items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from "people with knowledge of the matter".

Key things I learned from the article:

  • Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn"
  • Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn
  • Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn
  • In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power"
  • Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11%

This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine):

The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.

When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending.

Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter!

Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" (previously) in these communications to their investors.

items.title: LaTeX renderer
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office, which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner).

Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link.

Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used:

I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too.

Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks:

Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project

I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well:

We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool

items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).

I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to  software. [...]

This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[

With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is  news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.

This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.

"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion.

They had some pretty extreme requirements:

The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a  working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.

When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied:

Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do.

As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:

Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.

Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.

When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.

(I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)

items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.

First, some highlights from Python 3.15.

The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.
My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as  could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the  command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.
 [[, ], [, ], []]
[]
 [{, }, {, }, {, }]
{}
 [{: }, {: }, {: }]
{}

Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from  to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.
Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.
If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use  on macOS):
sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234
Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:
3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14
Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.
Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.
Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv
I used the following sequence of commands to get  to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade  itself to ensure it knew about the new release:
Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:
And told  that I wanted that to be the default for every  command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:
uv python pin --global 3.15
Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:
I already have a bunch of tools installed using . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:
uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15
Then I can confirm the version like this:
datasette --get /-/versions.json  jq
Highlights from Python 3.11
The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.
My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.
 is a new in 3.11 alias for .
Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:
  • create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with , , , and  methods.
  • blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large  binary values stored in a SQLite row.
  • You can now call  to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!
I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that  workaround.

items.title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers.

Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog.)

The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year:

We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development.

Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News:

It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough.

I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development.

My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access.

items.title: Quoting Matthew Green

Everyone is very concerned about being respectable, so I’m going to be the goofball who raises worst-case possibilities. I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms. [...]

The problem here is that the speed of AI producing surprises, and the speed of human beings replacing standards (even with the very best AI assistance) are just orders of magnitude different. You only recover from a surprise like this if you do the preparation in advance.

items.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner.

I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like:

Start dev server and open in browser

This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress.

Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked.

I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources.

Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex:

Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results.

Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist.

We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code.

We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice:

  • A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that
  • Four working imports:
    • The most recent Substack items via RSS
    • Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner
    • My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository
  • Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage
  • Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages
  • Integration with my site search engine

It was ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while.

Finishing it with a review

Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request.

I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead.

You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR. I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR.

The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages.

GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen.

Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver

OpenAI using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though.

I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code.

This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent.

I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words.

I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace!

The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead.

items.title: Quoting Ben Affleck
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
I've always been kind of into computers since I was young. And then when film started to move from analog film to digital, I became more interested in that aspect of it. And the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning.

So I can write like pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that because with convolutional neural networks, which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do, which is just much more computation simultaneously, you would do things like look at what's called a tensor, which is just the numerical translation of a visual image in numbers — like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame.

And a tensor, you use a convolutional neural network to identify patterns in that that would reveal what's called edge detection or feature extraction, which is just identifying patterns enough to know like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.

items.title: Claude Haiku 5.5
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago, and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, released last month.

The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75.

Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there's a hidden price increase there.

If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal.

llm install -U llm-anthropic
llm anthropic refresh
llm -m claude-haiku-5.5 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" -o thinking_effort low

This effort pelican (with a reasoning trace that starts "This is the classic pelican-on-bicycle SVG test...") took 5 minutes 9 seconds to generate, but still only cost me 3.3826 cents:

For comparison, here's the pelican I got a year ago from Haiku 4.5 (for 0.7583 cents - Haiku 4.5 did not support reasoning levels). It at drawing pelicans:

And a generous API credit scheme for subscribers

In addition to Haiku 5.5, Anthropic announced today that they are halving the price of cache reads for Sonnet 5.5. They've also added API credits to subscription plans:

Second, this week, we’ll roll out a new monthly API credit to all Max and Team subscribers for use on the Claude Platform. Max 5x users will get $100 in credits per month, Max 20x users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users.

Claiming this is pleasantly easy: navigate to Settings -> Billing and select the API organization that should benefit from the credits every month:

The API credits exactly match the cost of the subscription itself. This is really generous - it makes it much easier for subscribers to use the API. Anthropic also let you disable auto-reload for the API, with the consequence that "API requests will stop when your balance runs out" - exactly what you want if you're planning to burn through those API credits without risk of a nasty billing surprise.

OpenAI still allow you to use your Codex subscription for personal API use, which works out as a better deal for heavy API users. This new credit scheme goes at least some way to overcoming that difference.

items.title: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
Some excellent writing advice from Michael Lynch. Michael warns against "meandering intros", misjudging your reader's existing knowledge, assuming they'll read your previous posts, and excessive formality.

He also warns against overreliance on links as an excuse not to explain terminology. This one hurt! I do this all the time, but I have a nagging suspicion that almost nobody ever clicks on them.

(In a Lobste.rs comment Michael clarifies that "My rule of thumb is that my article should still make sense to the reader even if they don't click any links". That works for me.)

This point about using your own voice is crucial:

Beginner software bloggers suffer from a mass delusion that you have to write in a stiff, overly formal way for people to take you seriously [...]

Just write the way you talk.

With so many developers delegating their writing to AI, software blogging is becoming bland and homogenous. Readers are hungry for writing with personality.

items.title: Quoting Jake Boggan
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
I was a graph theory junkie long ago and even moved to Budapest for awhile to study among the greats. While I was there I started working on Barnette's Conjecture which came to occupy my thoughts over the next 24 years of my life, on and off as I worked in many different fields. Last summer I even thought for a few days that I had actually solved it.

But it's supposedly proven here - problem 180. I don't know what to think exactly. I spent thousands of hours on that problem. I really enjoyed it. Hearing that it is solved somehow makes me sad in a far-off way, like hearing an ex-girlfriend died suddenly in a car crash. I don't know, there's probably a lot of people feeling odd emotions tonight.

items.title: OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects
items.author: Simon Willison
items.content:
Given how tempting a target wikis are for rogue agent swarms, it's not a huge surprise that Wikipedia found evidence of that activity once they went looking:

The Wikimedia Foundation conducted its own investigation to see whether Wikimedia websites had been similarly affected by AI agents, focusing on those operated by OpenAI. We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic, which are described more below.

They found evidence of agents editing sandbox pages, trying to use pieces of infrastructure such as Etherpad to help proxy content from elsewhere, and saw widespread crawling and "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to their Wikidata Query Service.

My best guess is that most of this was a similar (or the same) swarm of agents as those that defaced that German wiki while training for research tasks.

The Wikipedia sandbox wiki edits appear to have started on May 12th, and the initial test edits to the UseModWiki Sandbox page reported by that incident started on May 11th.

items.title: I am often wrong
items.content:
[I shared this note with my team earlier this week, and am posting it here as well. I hope it is interesting or helpful for others working on building product in the age of AI.]

Something that people learn quickly when they work with me is that my approach to pretty much every problem is:

  1. Understand the available information
  2. Gather missing information
  3. Define a clear and simple approach to solve the problem
  4. Act with urgency to achieve the goal

Along the way, I will often learn new information. That means going back and redefining #3-5, and repeating. This process is iterative and for complicated problems, it can take many tries to get right. This can feel thrashy, but if you are aware that it’s all part of the process, and that the only way to really solve a problem is to adjust when there is new data, then the churn is healthy. When there’s new data, you have to update your priors.

I apply something like these six steps for pretty much every problem, and pretty much every product (a product solves a problem for users). I apply this rough framework many times on most days.

Sometimes I will give feedback to people when they are missing steps in the framework, or are poorly executing some of the steps. I expect the same feedback in return. I try hard to give the feedback in real time, so the person/team can learn more quickly. Most often, the failure mode I see is (3) failure to clearly define the problem, and (4) failure to define an approach that is clear and simple. When one of these is missing, it leads to complex plans and unclear success criteria. For complicated problems, lack of clarity can be hard to spot if you’re the one making the plan, making it even more important to get feedback from people.

If part of this meta-process is meta-wrong, I am open to changing it.

All this to say, I love being wrong. It is my favorite, because it helps me more clearly define the problem, find the right solution, learn more quickly, and solve the problem.
